claim: About 100 heterochromatic TEs are activated in vegetative cells (VCs) of Arabidopsis thaliana pollen.
source: Here we show that about 100 heterochromatic TEs are activated in VCs, mostly by DEMETER-catalyzed DNA demethylation.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data identifying 114 TEs transcribed at significantly higher levels in pollen than rosette leaves, which are characterized as heterochromatic based on their genomic features and histone modifications.

claim: TE activation in VCs is mostly caused by DEMETER-catalyzed DNA demethylation.
source: Here we show that about 100 heterochromatic TEs are activated in VCs, mostly by DEMETER-catalyzed DNA demethylation.
evidence: The manuscript shows that 71 of 114 (62%) VC-activated TEs overlap VC DME targets at their TSSs, and RNA-seq of dme/+ heterozygous plants showed significantly reduced expression at VC-activated TEs.

claim: DEMETER access to some heterochromatic TEs is permitted by the natural depletion of linker histone H1 in VCs.
source: We further demonstrate that DEMETER access to some of these TEs is permitted by the natural depletion of linker histone H1 in VCs.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates through bisulfite sequencing that ectopic H1 expression in VCs causes hypermethylation at DME targets, particularly heterochromatic ones, indicating H1 normally impedes DME access.

claim: Ectopically expressed H1 suppresses TEs in VCs by reducing DNA demethylation.
source: Ectopically expressed H1 suppresses TEs in VCs by reducing DNA demethylation and via a methylation-independent mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript shows that 20 of 46 H1-repressed TEs show significant increase of DNA methylation within 500 bp of the TSS in pVC::H1.

claim: Ectopically expressed H1 suppresses TEs in VCs via a methylation-independent mechanism.
source: Ectopically expressed H1 suppresses TEs in VCs by reducing DNA demethylation and via a methylation-independent mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript shows that 21 out of 22 H1-repressed TEs do not overlap any H1 hyperDMRs within 500 bp of the TSS, indicating their suppression by H1 is not mediated by DNA methylation.

claim: H1 is required for heterochromatin condensation in plant cells.
source: We demonstrate that H1 is required for heterochromatin condensation in plant cells and show that H1 overexpression creates heterochromatic foci in the VC progenitor cell.
evidence: The manuscript shows through immunostaining that H1 co-localizes with H3K9me2 in chromocenters, and chromocenters become dispersed in h1 mutant rosette leaves.

claim: H1 overexpression creates heterochromatic foci in the VC progenitor cell (late microspore).
source: We demonstrate that H1 is required for heterochromatin condensation in plant cells and show that H1 overexpression creates heterochromatic foci in the VC progenitor cell.
evidence: The manuscript shows through confocal microscopy that strong chromocenters are observed in 68% of late microspores in pMSP1::H1 plants, compared to 27% in WT.

claim: Natural depletion of H1 during male gametogenesis facilitates DEMETER-directed DNA demethylation.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that the natural depletion of H1 during male gametogenesis facilitates DEMETER-directed DNA demethylation, heterochromatin relaxation, and TE activation.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates through bisulfite sequencing that ectopic H1 expression in VCs impedes DME activity at heterochromatic targets, showing that H1 absence normally facilitates DME access.

claim: Natural depletion of H1 during male gametogenesis facilitates heterochromatin relaxation.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that the natural depletion of H1 during male gametogenesis facilitates DEMETER-directed DNA demethylation, heterochromatin relaxation, and TE activation.
evidence: The manuscript shows that H1 is required for heterochromatin condensation in plant cells, and H1 depletion begins at the late microspore stage when chromocenters start to disperse.

claim: Natural depletion of H1 during male gametogenesis facilitates TE activation.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that the natural depletion of H1 during male gametogenesis facilitates DEMETER-directed DNA demethylation, heterochromatin relaxation, and TE activation.
evidence: The manuscript shows that ectopic H1 expression in VCs suppresses 46 out of 114 VC-activated TEs, demonstrating that H1 absence normally permits their activation.

claim: TEs comprise approximately 50% of the human genome.
source: For example, TEs comprise approximately 50% of the human genome (International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2001; Venter et al., 2001), and more than 85% of the genomes in crops such as wheat and maize (Schnable et al., 2009; Wicker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TEs comprise more than 85% of the genomes in crops such as wheat and maize.
source: For example, TEs comprise approximately 50% of the human genome (International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2001; Venter et al., 2001), and more than 85% of the genomes in crops such as wheat and maize (Schnable et al., 2009; Wicker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Activities of TEs compromise genome stability, disrupt functional genes, and are often associated with severe diseases including cancers in animals.
source: Regarded as selfish and parasitic, activities of TEs compromise genome stability, disrupt functional genes, and are often associated with severe diseases including cancers in animals (Anwar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Eukaryotic hosts have evolved efficient epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, to suppress TEs.
source: To safeguard genome integrity, eukaryotic hosts have evolved efficient epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, to suppress TEs (He et al., 2011; Law and Jacobsen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LINE-1 retrotransposons are highly expressed in pre-implantation embryos and the fetal germline despite relatively low levels of transposition.
source: In pre-implantation embryos and the fetal germline, LINE-1 retrotransposons are highly expressed despite relatively low levels of transposition (Fadloun et al., 2013; Kano et al., 2009; Percharde et al., 2017; Richardson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LINE-1 RNA plays a key regulatory role in promoting pre-implantation embryo development in mice.
source: Recently, LINE-1 RNA was shown to play a key regulatory role in promoting pre-implantation embryo development in mice (Percharde et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: LINE-1 elements transcribe and mobilize in neuronal precursor cells in mice and human.
source: LINE-1 elements have also been shown to transcribe and mobilize in neuronal precursor cells in mice and human (Coufal et al., 2009; Muotri et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hypomethylation at LINE-1 promoters in neurons has been proposed to contribute to TE activation.
source: Hypomethylation at LINE-1 promoters in neurons has been proposed to contribute (Coufal et al., 2009), and possibly the availability of transcription factors (Muotri et al., 2005; Richardson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Each microspore undergoes an asymmetric mitosis to generate a bicellular pollen comprised of a large vegetative cell (VC) and a small generative cell engulfed by the VC.
source: Each microspore undergoes an asymmetric mitosis to generate a bicellular pollen comprised of a large vegetative cell (VC) and a small generative cell engulfed by the VC (Berger and Twell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established knowledge about plant reproduction.

claim: The generative cell divides again mitotically to produce two sperm.
source: Subsequently the generative cell divides again mitotically to produce two sperm.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about plant reproduction.

claim: Upon pollination, the VC develops into a pollen tube to deliver the sperm to meet the female cells, and subsequently degenerates.
source: Upon pollination, the VC develops into a pollen tube to deliver the sperm to meet the female cells, and subsequently degenerates.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about plant reproduction.

claim: Several TEs were found activated and transposed in the mature tricellular pollen of Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: In the mature tricellular pollen of Arabidopsis thaliana, several TEs were found activated and transposed (Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TE activation in pollen is confined to the VC.
source: Enhancer/gene trap insertions into TEs showed specific reporter activity in the VC, and TE transpositions detected in pollen were absent in progeny (Slotkin et al., 2009). These results demonstrated TE activation in pollen is confined to the VC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TE expression in the short-lived VC has been proposed to promote the production of small RNAs, which may be transported into sperm to reinforce the silencing of cognate TEs.
source: TE expression in the short-lived VC has been proposed to promote the production of small RNAs, which may be transported into sperm to reinforce the silencing of cognate TEs (Calarco et al., 2012; Ibarra et al., 2012; Martínez et al., 2016; Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and represents a hypothesis.

claim: DDM1 functions to overcome the impediment of nucleosomes and linker histone H1 to DNA methyltransferases.
source: DDM1 functions to overcome the impediment of nucleosomes and linker histone H1 to DNA methyltransferases (Lyons and Zilberman, 2017; Zemach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of DDM1 leads to DNA hypomethylation and massive TE derepression in somatic tissues.
source: Loss of DDM1 leads to DNA hypomethylation and massive TE derepression in somatic tissues (Jeddeloh et al., 1999; Lippman et al., 2004; Tsukahara et al., 2009; Zemach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Global DNA methylation in the VC is comparable to that of microspores and substantially higher than in somatic tissues.
source: However, global DNA methylation in the VC is comparable to that of microspores and substantially higher than in somatic tissues (Calarco et al., 2012; Hsieh et al., 2016; Ibarra et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Approximately ten thousand loci – predominantly TEs – are hypomethylated in the VC, primarily in the CG context and to a lesser extent in the CHG/H contexts.
source: Approximately ten thousand loci – predominantly TEs – are hypomethylated in the VC, primarily in the CG context and to a lesser extent in the CHG/H contexts (Calarco et al., 2012; Ibarra et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hypomethylation in the VC is caused by a DNA glycosylase called DEMETER (DME).
source: Hypomethylation in the VC is caused by a DNA glycosylase called DEMETER (DME) (Ibarra et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: DME demethylates DNA via direct excision of methylated cytosine.
source: DME demethylates DNA via direct excision of methylated cytosine, and its expression is confined to the VC and its female counterpart, the central cell, during sexual reproduction (Choi et al., 2002; Schoft et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DME expression is confined to the VC and its female counterpart, the central cell, during sexual reproduction.
source: DME demethylates DNA via direct excision of methylated cytosine, and its expression is confined to the VC and its female counterpart, the central cell, during sexual reproduction (Choi et al., 2002; Schoft et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Centromeric repeats are condensed in sperm and other cell types but are decondensed in the VC.
source: For example, centromeric repeats, which are condensed in sperm and other cell types, are decondensed in the VC, accompanied by the depletion of centromeric histone H3 (Ingouff et al., 2010; Mérai et al., 2014; Schoft et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Chromocenters are observed in sperm nuclei but absent in the VC nucleus.
source: Chromocenters, which are comprised of condensed pericentromeric heterochromatin and rDNA repeats (Chandrasekhara et al., 2016; Fransz et al., 2002; Tessadori et al., 2004), are observed in sperm nuclei but absent in the VC nucleus, suggesting that pericentromeric heterochromatin is decondensed in the VC (Baroux et al., 2011; Ingouff et al., 2010; Schoft et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Heterochromatin decondensation in the VC is proposed to promote rDNA transcription that empowers pollen tube growth.
source: Heterochromatin decondensation in the VC is proposed to promote rDNA transcription that empowers pollen tube growth (Mérai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Histone H1 is depleted in Arabidopsis VC nuclei.
source: Our previous work showed that histone H1, which binds to the nucleosome surface and the linker DNA between two adjacent nucleosomes (Fyodorov et al., 2018), is depleted in Arabidopsis VC nuclei (Hsieh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: H1 depletion in the VC has been observed in a distantly related lily species.
source: H1 depletion in the VC has also been observed in a distantly related lily species (Tanaka et al., 1998), suggesting a conserved phenomenon in flowering plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: H1 contributes to heterochromatin condensation in Drosophila and mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: In Drosophila and mouse embryonic stem cells, H1 has been shown to contribute to heterochromatin condensation (Cao et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: H1 is more abundant in heterochromatin than euchromatin in Arabidopsis.
source: H1 is also more abundant in heterochromatin than euchromatin in Arabidopsis (Ascenzi and Gantt, 1999; Rutowicz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the central cell, the histone chaperone FACT is required for DME-directed DNA demethylation in heterochromatic TEs, and this requirement is dependent on H1.
source: In the central cell, the histone chaperone FACT (facilitates chromatin transactions) is required for DME-directed DNA demethylation in heterochromatic TEs, and this requirement is dependent on H1 (Frost et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: DME activity in the VC is independent of FACT.
source: However, DME activity in the VC is independent of FACT (Frost et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: 114 TEs are transcribed at significantly higher levels in pollen than rosette leaves.
source: We identified 114 TEs that are transcribed at significantly higher levels in pollen than rosette leaves (fold change >2; p<0.05, likelihood ratio test), and hence likely to be specifically activated in the VC (Figure 1—source data 1) (Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data analyzed using Mikado, Kallisto, and Sleuth to identify these TEs.

claim: VC-activated TEs are primarily located in pericentromeric regions.
source: The VC-activated TEs are primarily located in pericentromeric regions and exhibit features of heterochromatic TEs, such as being long and GC rich (Frost et al., 2018) (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents chromosomal distribution data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VC-activated TEs are long and GC rich.
source: The VC-activated TEs are primarily located in pericentromeric regions and exhibit features of heterochromatic TEs, such as being long and GC rich (Frost et al., 2018) (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents box plots in Figure 1B showing length and GC content of VC-activated TEs compared to all TEs.

claim: VC-activated TEs are significantly enriched in dimethylation of histone H3 on lysine 9 (H3K9me2) in somatic tissues.
source: As is typical of heterochromatic TEs (Zemach et al., 2013), VC-activated TEs are significantly enriched in dimethylation of histone H3 on lysine 9 (H3K9me2) in somatic tissues, and are significantly depleted of euchromatin-associated modifications (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents box plots in Figure 1B showing H3K9me2 enrichment at VC-activated TEs.

claim: VC-activated TEs are significantly depleted of euchromatin-associated modifications.
source: As is typical of heterochromatic TEs (Zemach et al., 2013), VC-activated TEs are significantly enriched in dimethylation of histone H3 on lysine 9 (H3K9me2) in somatic tissues, and are significantly depleted of euchromatin-associated modifications (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents box plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing depletion of euchromatic histone modifications at VC-activated TEs.

claim: MuDR DNA transposons and Gypsy LTR-retrotransposons are significantly overrepresented among VC-activated TEs.
source: VC-activated TEs encompass diverse TE families, among which MuDR DNA transposons and Gypsy LTR-retrotransposons are significantly overrepresented (p<10−9 and 0.01, respectively, Fisher's exact test; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) of TE family composition shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VC-activated TEs have substantially lower CG methylation in the VC than in sperm at and near the TSS.
source: We found that these TEs have substantially lower CG methylation in the VC than in sperm at and near the TSS (Figure 1D,E), indicative of DME activity.
evidence: The manuscript presents bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1D,E demonstrating differential methylation.

claim: DNA methylation in VCs from dme/+ heterozygous plants shows an intermediate level of methylation at TSS and TTS of VC-activated TEs.
source: Examination of DNA methylation in VCs from dme/+ heterozygous plants (dme homozygous mutants are embryonic lethal), which produce a 50:50 ratio of dme mutant and WT pollen, revealed an intermediate level of methylation at TSS and TTS of VC-activated TEs (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript presents bisulfite sequencing data from dme/+ VCs shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: CHG and CHH methylation is substantially increased at the TSS (and TTS) of VC-activated TEs in dme/+ VC.
source: CHG and CHH methylation is also substantially increased at the TSS (and TTS) of VC-activated TEs in dme/+ VC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the knowledge that DME demethylates all sequence contexts (Gehring et al., 2006; Ibarra et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript presents bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and cites published literature about DME activity.

claim: 71 of the 114 (62%) VC-activated TEs overlap VC DME targets at their TSSs.
source: Consistent with the above results, 71 of the 114 (62%) VC-activated TEs overlap VC DME targets at their TSSs (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of overlap between VC-activated TEs and DME targets shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 92 out of the 114 TEs (81%) have VC DME targets within 500 bp of the TSS.
source: 92 out of the 114 TEs (81%) have VC DME targets within 500 bp of the TSS (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of proximity between VC-activated TEs and DME targets shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: RNA-seq of pollen from dme/+ heterozygous plants showed significantly reduced expression at the 114 VC-activated TEs.
source: Consistently, RNA-seq of pollen from dme/+ heterozygous plants showed significantly reduced expression at the 114 VC-activated TEs (Figure 1G, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data from dme/+ pollen shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The median ratio of transcription of VC-activated TEs in dme/+ versus WT pollen is 0.43.
source: The 114 VC-activated TEs are transcribed at levels close to this expectation (Figure 1G), with the median ratio of their transcription in dme/+ versus WT pollen being 0.43 (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: H1.1 and H1.2 are present in early microspore nucleus but absent in the late microspore stage.
source: H1.1- and H1.2- GFP reporters exhibit the same expression pattern: present in early microspore nucleus but absent in the late microspore stage, and remaining absent in the VC nucleus while present in the generative cell and subsequent sperm nuclei (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images of H1-GFP reporters shown in Figure 2A.

claim: H1.1 and H1.2 remain absent in the VC nucleus while present in the generative cell and subsequent sperm nuclei.
source: H1.1- and H1.2- GFP reporters exhibit the same expression pattern: present in early microspore nucleus but absent in the late microspore stage, and remaining absent in the VC nucleus while present in the generative cell and subsequent sperm nuclei (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images of H1-GFP reporters shown in Figure 2A.

claim: H1.3 is not detectable in either microspore or pollen.
source: H1.3 is not detectable in either microspore or pollen (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images of H1.3-GFP reporter shown in Figure 2A.

claim: H1 depletion begins at the late microspore stage.
source: These results are consistent with our previous observations, confirming that H1 is absent in the VC (Hsieh et al., 2016), and demonstrating that H1 depletion begins at the late microspore stage.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy data showing H1 presence in early microspores but absence in late microspores.

claim: H1 expression in VC leads to shortened siliques.
source: Notably, we found H1 expression in VC leads to shortened siliques, a substantial proportion of malformed pollen, and reduced pollen germination rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting the depletion of H1 in the VC is important for pollen fertility.
evidence: The manuscript presents phenotypic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H1 expression in VC leads to a substantial proportion of malformed pollen.
source: Notably, we found H1 expression in VC leads to shortened siliques, a substantial proportion of malformed pollen, and reduced pollen germination rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting the depletion of H1 in the VC is important for pollen fertility.
evidence: The manuscript presents phenotypic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: H1 expression in VC leads to reduced pollen germination rate.
source: Notably, we found H1 expression in VC leads to shortened siliques, a substantial proportion of malformed pollen, and reduced pollen germination rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting the depletion of H1 in the VC is important for pollen fertility.
evidence: The manuscript presents pollen germination data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The depletion of H1 in the VC is important for pollen fertility.
source: Notably, we found H1 expression in VC leads to shortened siliques, a substantial proportion of malformed pollen, and reduced pollen germination rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting the depletion of H1 in the VC is important for pollen fertility.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ectopic H1 expression causes fertility defects.

claim: CG methylation in the VC of pVC::H1 plants is largely similar to that of WT, except for a slight increase in TE methylation.
source: CG methylation in the VC of pVC::H1 plants is largely similar to that of WT, except for a slight increase in TE methylation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A substantial proportion of loci that are targeted by DME show hypermethylation in pVC::H1 VC.
source: However, a substantial proportion of loci that are targeted by DME show hypermethylation in pVC::H1 VC (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents kernel density plots shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: DME targets show preferential hypermethylation in CHG and CHH contexts in the VC of pVC::H1.
source: DME targets also show preferential hypermethylation in CHG and CHH contexts in the VC of pVC::H1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents kernel density plots shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: 2964 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are significantly CG hypermethylated in the VC of pVC::H1 plants.
source: Across the genome, we found 2964 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) that are significantly CG hypermethylated in the VC of pVC::H1 plants (referred to as H1 hyperDMRs hereafter; ranging from 101 to 2155 nt in length, 280 nt on average; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents bisulfite sequencing data analysis identifying H1 hyperDMRs.

claim: Most of the H1 hyperDMRs (1618, 55%) overlap DME targets in the VC.
source: Most of the H1 hyperDMRs (1618, 55%) overlap DME targets in the VC (Figure 2—source data 1), and H1 hyperDMRs exhibit strong hypomethylation in WT VCs, with 81.4% (2412 sites) having significantly more CG methylation in sperm than VC (p<0.001, Fisher's exact test), indicating that most H1 hyperDMRs are DME targets (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of overlap between H1 hyperDMRs and DME targets, and methylation data shown in Figure 2E–H.

claim: 81.4% (2412 sites) of H1 hyperDMRs have significantly more CG methylation in sperm than VC.
source: Most of the H1 hyperDMRs (1618, 55%) overlap DME targets in the VC (Figure 2—source data 1), and H1 hyperDMRs exhibit strong hypomethylation in WT VCs, with 81.4% (2412 sites) having significantly more CG methylation in sperm than VC (p<0.001, Fisher's exact test), indicating that most H1 hyperDMRs are DME targets (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis of methylation differences shown in Figure 2E–H.

claim: Only 3066 out of 11896 (26%) VC DME targets have significantly more CG methylation in the VC of pVC::H1 than WT.
source: However, only 3066 out of 11896 (26%) VC DME targets have significantly more CG methylation in the VC of pVC::H1 than WT (p<0.001, Fisher's exact test; Figure 1—source data 2), indicating that VC-expressed H1 impedes DME at a minority of its genomic targets.
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis of methylation differences at DME targets.

claim: H1-impeded DME targets are heterochromatic and significantly enriched in H3K9me2 compared with H1-independent DME targets.
source: These H1-impeded DME targets are heterochromatic and significantly enriched in H3K9me2 compared with H1-independent DME targets (Figure 2I).
evidence: The manuscript presents box plot analysis shown in Figure 2I comparing H3K9me2 levels.

claim: pVC::H1-induced hypermethylation is apparent only in the most heterochromatic group (highest H3K9me2) of DME target loci.
source: pVC::H1-induced hypermethylation peaks where DME-mediated hypomethylation peaks, but is apparent only in the most heterochromatic group (highest H3K9me2) of DME target loci (Figure 2J).
evidence: The manuscript presents meta-analysis shown in Figure 2J demonstrating H1 effects on different groups of DME targets.

claim: Only a small fraction of pollen-expressed genes (3%; 89 out of 2845) is differentially expressed between pVC::H1 and WT.
source: Only a small fraction of pollen-expressed genes (3%; 89 out of 2845) is differentially expressed (fold change >2; p<0.05, likelihood ratio test) between pVC::H1 and WT (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Among the 89 differentially expressed genes, 58 (65%) are suppressed by H1 expression in the VC, and 31 (35%) are activated.
source: Among these 89 genes, 58 (65%) are suppressed by H1 expression in the VC, and 31 (35%) are activated (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 85 out of 89 differentially expressed genes (96%) do not overlap DME targets within 500 bp of the TSS.
source: 85 out of these 89 genes (96%) do not overlap DME targets within 500 bp of the TSS, hence the effect of H1 on their expression is probably not mediated by DME.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of overlap between differentially expressed genes and DME targets.

claim: DME targets likely regulating imprinted genes are associated with significantly less H1 in somatic tissues than the VC DME targets that are dependent on H1.
source: Consistently, DME targets likely regulating imprinted genes are associated with significantly less H1 in somatic tissues than the VC DME targets that are dependent on H1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents box plot analysis shown in Figure 3C comparing H1 occupancy.

claim: A substantial proportion of VC-activated TEs (41%; 47 out of 114) show significant differential expression due to H1 expression in VC.
source: In contrast to the small effect of H1 on gene transcription, a substantial proportion of VC-activated TEs (41%; 47 out of 114) show significant differential expression (fold change >2; p<0.05, likelihood ratio test) due to H1 expression in VC (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Among the differentially expressed TEs, the overwhelming majority (46; 98%) are repressed by H1.
source: Among these differentially expressed TEs, the overwhelming majority (46; 98%) are repressed (Figure 3D,E, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: H1 represses TE expression in a dosage-dependent manner.
source: Taking advantage of a pVC::H1 line #7 with weaker H1 expression in pollen (Figure 3A), we found H1 represses TE expression in a dosage-dependent manner: TEs are suppressed to a lesser extent in line #7 compared to the strong line #2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript presents qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A and 3F comparing two lines with different H1 expression levels.

claim: H1-repressed TEs in the VC are predominantly localized to pericentromeric regions.
source: H1-repressed TEs in the VC are predominantly localized to pericentromeric regions and are overrepresented for LTR retrotransposons, including Gypsy and Copia elements (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents chromosomal distribution data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: H1-repressed TEs are overrepresented for LTR retrotransposons, including Gypsy and Copia elements.
source: H1-repressed TEs in the VC are predominantly localized to pericentromeric regions and are overrepresented for LTR retrotransposons, including Gypsy and Copia elements (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents TE family composition data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: H1-repressed TEs are significantly longer and enriched for H3K9me2 and H1 in somatic tissues compared to other VC-activated TEs.
source: Compared to other VC-activated TEs, the H1-repressed TEs are significantly longer and enriched for H3K9me2 and H1 in somatic tissues (Figure 3H), consistent with the observation that H1 precludes DME access to heterochromatin.
evidence: The manuscript presents box plot analysis shown in Figure 3H comparing genomic features.

claim: 20 of 46 H1-repressed TEs show significant increase of DNA methylation in at least one sequence context within 500 bp of the TSS in pVC::H1.
source: In support of the hypothesis that H1 represses VC TE expression by blocking DME, 20 of 46 H1-repressed TEs show significant increase of DNA methylation in at least one sequence context within 500 bp of the TSS in pVC::H1 (p<0.001, Fisher's exact test; Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The manuscript presents methylation analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: 21 out of 22 H1-repressed TEs that do not show increased methylation do not overlap any H1 hyperDMRs within 500 bp of the TSS.
source: However, 21 out of the rest of 22 TEs do not overlap any H1 hyperDMRs within 500 bp of the TSS (Figure 4A, marked by asterisks in the lower panel), indicating that their suppression by H1 is not mediated by DNA methylation.
evidence: The manuscript presents methylation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H1 co-localizes with H3K9me2 in highly-compacted heterochromatic foci (chromocenters) in leaf nuclei.
source: Immunostaining of leaf nuclei showed that H1 co-localizes with H3K9me2 in highly-compacted heterochromatic foci, known as chromocenters (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Chromocenters become dispersed in the nuclei of h1 mutant rosette leaves.
source: Furthermore, we found that chromocenters become dispersed in the nuclei of h1 mutant rosette leaves (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No condensed chromocenters are detected in WT VC.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Baroux et al., 2011; Ingouff et al., 2010; Schoft et al., 2009), no condensed chromocenters were detected in WT VC (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and cites previous observations.

claim: pVC::H1 VC show no obvious chromocenters.
source: pVC::H1 VC also showed no obvious chromocenters (n > 500; Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy observations.

claim: Chromocenters are observed at early microspore stage, but become dispersed in late microspore stage.
source: Heterochromatin decondensation during male gametogenesis seems to be gradual: chromocenters are observed at early microspore stage, but become dispersed in late microspore stage, when H1 is depleted (Figures 2A and 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 2A and 5C.

claim: Strong and weak chromocenters are observed in 27% and 59% of late microspore nuclei, respectively.
source: We observed strong and weak chromocenters, respectively, in 27% and 59% of late microspore nuclei, whereas no chromocenters were observed in the VC at either bicellular or tricellular pollen stage (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of chromocenter observations shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: No chromocenters are observed in the VC at either bicellular or tricellular pollen stage.
source: We observed strong and weak chromocenters, respectively, in 27% and 59% of late microspore nuclei, whereas no chromocenters were observed in the VC at either bicellular or tricellular pollen stage (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of chromocenter observations shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Strong chromocenters are observed in the majority (68%) of late microspores in pMSP1::H1.
source: In pMSP1::H1, we observed strong chromocenters in the majority (68%) of late microspores (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of chromocenter observations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: H1 expression in pMSP1::H1 is specific to late microspores, and co-localizes with induced chromocenters.
source: H1 expression in pMSP1::H1 is specific to late microspores, and co-localizes with induced chromocenters (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: H1 is sufficient to promote heterochromatic foci in late microspores.
source: These results show that H1 is sufficient to promote heterochromatic foci in late microspores, thus demonstrating the causal relationship between H1 depletion and the decondensation of heterochromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ectopic H1 expression in late microspores induces chromocenters.

claim: DNA methylation at the TSS suppresses the transcription of genes and TEs in plants and animals.
source: As DNA methylation at/near the TSS has been well-demonstrated to suppress the transcription of genes and TEs in plants and animals (Barau et al., 2016; Eichten et al., 2012; Hollister and Gaut, 2009; Manakov et al., 2015; Meng et al., 2016), our results indicate that DME-directed demethylation is a major mechanism of TE activation in the VC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: H1 depletion causes local hypomethylation in mouse cells.
source: H1 depletion causes local hypomethylation in mouse cells (Fan et al., 2005) and extensive hypermethylation in the fungi Ascobolus immersus (Barra et al., 2000) and Neurospora crassa (Seymour et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: H1 depletion causes extensive hypermethylation in the fungi Ascobolus immersus and Neurospora crassa.
source: H1 depletion causes local hypomethylation in mouse cells (Fan et al., 2005) and extensive hypermethylation in the fungi Ascobolus immersus (Barra et al., 2000) and Neurospora crassa (Seymour et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of H1 causes global heterochromatic hypermethylation in all sequence contexts in Arabidopsis by allowing greater access of DNA methyltransferases.
source: In Arabidopsis, loss of H1 causes global heterochromatic hypermethylation in all sequence contexts by allowing greater access of DNA methyltransferases (Lyons and Zilberman, 2017; Zemach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: H1 may influence DME-homologous demethylases that control methylation in somatic tissues.
source: Our results suggest that H1 may also influence DME-homologous demethylases that control methylation in somatic tissues (He et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed effects of H1 on DME activity in the VC.

claim: H1 may serve as an integrator of methylation pathways that tunes methylation up or down depending on the locus.
source: By regulating both methylation and demethylation, H1 may serve as an integrator of methylation pathways that tunes methylation up or down depending on the locus.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed dual effects of H1 on methylation and demethylation.

claim: DNA methylation and H1 cooperate to suppress TE expression in plants.
source: Group III also demonstrates that DNA methylation and H1 cooperate to suppress TE expression in plants.
evidence: The manuscript shows that some TEs require both H1 depletion and DME demethylation for activation.

claim: TE activation in the VC may facilitate both host defense and transposition, with the balance specific to each TE family and changing over evolutionary time.
source: TE activation in the VC may facilitate both host defense and transposition, with the balance specific to each TE family and changing over evolutionary time.
evidence: This is speculated based on the discussion of competing hypotheses about the function of TE activation.
